# Comparative advantage

## Comparative advantage

A country has an absolute advantage in a good if it can produce more of it with the same resources than another country can. A country has a comparative advantage if its opportunity cost of producing a good is lower than that of another country. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that is given up. Countries gain from trade when each specialises in the good in which it has a comparative advantage. Absolute advantage alone does not determine which country should produce a good.

## Example

Suppose country A can produce 10 cars or 20 tonnes of wheat with a year of labour. Suppose country B can produce 6 cars or 18 tonnes of wheat with the same labour. Country A gives up 2 tonnes of wheat for each car, while country B gives up 3 tonnes of wheat for each car. Country A therefore has the comparative advantage in cars even though it is also better at wheat in absolute terms.
